titleEn: When You're Done, Hang It Up!

pages.text: "All done!" Dingding came up from the paddy and tossed their hat, water jug, and bamboo basket into the yard. Grandma, who had farmed rice all her life, called from behind, "Put away the things you used." "No, later! I want to play!"

On the way to wash at the basin, Dingding stepped on the basket's rim. "Ouch!" Dingding lifted one foot, then slipped on the hat and landed on the dirt with a thump. Everywhere in the yard seemed to hurt their feet.
And the water jug was missing. "Where did it go?" Dingding looked behind the basin and the wooden tub, but it was not there. Dingding was thirsty. Their eyes grew wet, and their nose began to sting.
Mom, who worked several paddies on her own, sat beside Dingding. "Why the sad face?" "My water jug is gone..." Mom pointed at the wall by the doorway. "I'll show you a good place."

Three hooks stood side by side on the wall. Mom tapped them. "A place for the hat, a place for the jug, and a place for the basket. When You're Done, Hang It Up! Then your feet won't hurt, and missing things will turn up." Dingding stared at the three empty hooks.
Dingding lifted the upside-down basket in the yard. Oh! The water jug was lying underneath. "My jug!"

"The missing thing turned up!" Dingding put the hat on the first hook and the jug on the second. Then the basket went on the third. All three hooks were full. Mom and Dingding sang, "When You're Done, Hang It Up!"
The yard was clear. Nothing lay underfoot to trip over. Dingding sniffed the refreshing smell of dry soil. "The yard got so much bigger!" Dingding spread their arms.
"One, go to the hooks when I come back! Two, hang up the hat, jug, and basket! Three, then play!" The next day, Dingding went straight to the hooks after work. "When You're Done, Hang It Up!"
Grandma hugged Dingding. "You're the captain of the hooks!" Hanging things in their places meant nothing to lose or step on. Dingding chuckled. "When You're Done, Hang It Up!"
